papers.title: When curiosity gaps backfire: effects of headline concreteness on information selection decisions
papers.study_kind: Registered report; multilevel meta-analysis of randomized field package tests with observational feature moderator
papers.scope: English Upworthy 2013–2015 article headline/image previews; website visitors; clicks per impression. Individual knowledge, curiosity, comprehension and quality not measured.
papers.sample_and_design: Pilot followed by held-out confirmatory archive subset; split image-varying tests into one-image bundles, retain bundles with at least two scorable distinct headlines; binomial random-intercept/slope model for headline score nested within test; mean test concreteness interacts with within-test deviation. Randomized assignment is to complete packages, not controlled random assignment of concreteness or mean test concreteness. Same original test may yield multiple image bundles.
outcomes: CTR on a preview, not article comprehension or durable engagement
concreteness proxy validated against mean human ratings

findings.claim: 35,910 headline-package observations (31,077 unique headlines) in 8,977 valid one-image bundles after 17,867 confirmatory tests and 85,830 packages; 70,546 scorable, 82.2%.
findings.interpretation_limits: Paper says 70,546 pilot headlines within confirmatory paragraph; likely textual inconsistency, not silently corrected. Bundles need not be independent original tests.

findings.claim: The interaction of headline concreteness with test mean was −0.058 (95% CI −0.091 to −0.025; Holm-adjusted p < 0.0013).
findings.interpretation_limits: Model-based association in randomized full-headline comparisons; other wording covaries, and mean is constructed from the test alternatives.

findings.claim: Estimated positive slope below test mean 2.58 (8.7% of tests), negative above 3.06 (50.9%); middle slopes not significantly distinct from zero.
findings.interpretation_limits: These are conditional confidence boundaries in this model, not validated universal cutoffs or an experimentally measured optimum for an individual author or reader.

findings.claim: 320 sampled headlines received 3,565 ratings; 176 final raters, average 11 ratings per headline; correlation between mean judgments and algorithm r=0.61.
findings.interpretation_limits: Moderate association does not establish meaning, truth, informativeness or coverage; excluded unscorable words threaten transfer to technical terms.

findings.claim: Prior nine reported experimental contrasts included three negative significant, two positive significant, four not distinguished from chance.
findings.denominator: 9 contrasts drawn from studies with differing outcome scales
findings.interpretation_limits: Narrative accounting of heterogeneous contrasts; not nine independent samples or pooled effect.

limitations: Score uses lexical concreteness, NER assigns entities maximum, excludes headlines with unmatched words ≥3 characters; removes 17.1% of headlines (p4).
Same article A/B estimates causal package contrasts but not causal interventions on concreteness or the cross-test average; inference rests on model and unmeasured co-varying features.
US English audience, one publisher, editorial selection and historical algorithm environment; no individual-level curiosity measurement.
p5 defines CTR backwards as impressions/clicks; p3 correctly defines clicks/impressions; p8 prose contradicts low/high example direction and values 4.37 versus 4.41.
data_or_code_leads: https://osf.io/fbzvw/ (paper analysis code; not independently audited)
https://github.com/maubinle/sentence_concreteness (paper names package; no install or license audit)
https://upworthy.natematias.com (archive access on request per p10)
extraction_issues: p5 inverse CTR formula contradicts p3; p6 pilot/confirmatory wording inconsistency; p8 upper-bound example reverses score descriptions.

papers.title: Linguistic effects on news headline success: Evidence from thousands of online field experiments (Registered Report)
papers.study_kind: Registered predictive and regression analysis of randomized field headline tests
papers.scope: Upworthy article headline alternatives with matched image and week; clickthrough winner classification.
papers.sample_and_design: Pilot 5,048 eligible pairs and 24,333 confirmatory pairs, selected within same article/image/week and significant after Bonferroni correction; disjoint headline pairings but multiple pairs may originate in a single experiment. Model trained on pilot evaluated on confirmatory for prediction; separate confirmatory coefficient regression. Whole headlines randomized, linguistic attributes not individually assigned. Selection on significance and ranking changes target population.
outcomes: binary higher-CTR headline in filtered pairs
feature associations in logistic model; not reader understanding or downstream behavior

findings.claim: Held-out prediction accuracy 54.42%, 99% CI 53.6%–55.2%, against balanced 50% baseline; recall 53.17%, precision 54.53%.
findings.interpretation_limits: Predicts a binary winner in statistically significant selected same-image/week pairs, not all headline tests; pairs can share experiments.

findings.claim: Negative-emotion indicator β=0.18 and headline-length comparison β=0.07; positive-emotion β=−0.04 and Flesch β=0.02 did not meet preregistered p<0.01.
findings.interpretation_limits: Coefficients are joint logistic pairwise winner associations, not estimated per-word or per-character CTR effects; other language differences remain.

findings.claim: Indefinite article β=0.12, first-person singular β=0.24, first-person plural β=−0.15; second-person β=0.05 did not meet p<0.01.
findings.interpretation_limits: Article/pronoun indicators are imperfect proxies; no universal prescription or author-voice judgment.

findings.claim: Seven of eleven feature hypotheses supported, four not supported at preregistered threshold.
findings.interpretation_limits: Non-significant is not proof of no effect; hypothesis outcomes are not independent replications.

limitations: Matched same image and time improve headline contrast; word-level effects remain modeled associations because variants differ on multiple correlated/unmeasured features (pp16–17).
Headline uniqueness across pairs does not guarantee statistical independence of tests, stories or users; archive aggregates impressions without individual identifiers.
Selection of significant pairs introduces winner-selection/generalization limitations. Topic, reader demographics, other forms and modern context differ.
P12 prose definite article p=0.0331 whereas Table 3 coefficient 0.0331 and p=0.123; avoid asserting disputed value.
data_or_code_leads: https://github.com/shivam5992/textstat (cited reference; not inspected or installed)
LIWC dictionary under separate terms; no reuse permission inferred
extraction_issues: p12 definite-article p-value inconsistent between text and table; p10 reports accuracy CI 0.536–0.552 while also reporting odds ratio; interpreted as accuracy interval.

papers.title: Negativity drives online news consumption
papers.study_kind: Registered report; multilevel analysis of randomized field headline/package experiments
papers.scope: Upworthy English viral-news headline previews, 2013–2015; aggregate CTR.
papers.sample_and_design: Confirmatory release: 22,743 experiments before filtering; exclude single headline tests, combine duplicate headlines including across images; 12,448 remaining experiments. Binomial model random intercepts and varying slopes with length, fog index, positive/negative lexical scores, time. Whole variants randomized; emotion tokens are post hoc attributes, not randomized word interventions. Archive aggregates headline impressions and clicks, not individual users; independence across experiments asserted by authors but repeated users cannot be tested.
outcomes: clicks per impression; no direct measurement of sentiment, comprehension, satisfaction, share or writing quality

findings.claim: After filtering: 12,448 experiments, 53,699 headline variations, more than 205 million impressions and 2,778,124 clicks; mean 4.31 variants per experiment.
findings.interpretation_limits: Figure 2 caption reports 53,669, whereas text and Table 3 report 53,699.

findings.claim: Negative score β=0.015, 99% CI 0.013–0.018 per standardized proportion; authors estimate 2.3% relative CTR increase for each additional negative word at average 14.965-word headline.
findings.evidence_locator: Effect of negative language; model standardization
findings.interpretation_limits: Not 2.3 percentage points; model estimate rather than randomized isolated-word substitution; lexical choices and other wording may change together.

findings.claim: Positive score β=−0.008 (99% CI −0.010 to −0.006); authors estimate 1.0% relative CTR decrease per positive word for mean-length headline.
findings.interpretation_limits: P07 found no support for its positive-word hypothesis; different selection, estimands, modeling and lexicon processing on overlapping archive.

findings.claim: Secondary discrete-emotion scores: sadness β=0.006; fear β=−0.007; joy β=−0.009; anger β≈0, p=0.666 and equivalence test inconclusive.
findings.denominator: same filtered corpus, modeled dictionary emotion proportions
findings.interpretation_limits: Fear sign opposes preregistered hypothesis; non-significant anger does not establish no effect. Different outcome from sharing; emotion label is lexical proxy.

findings.claim: Varying-slope model: negative β=0.018 (99% CI 0.011–0.025), positive β=−0.017 (−0.023 to −0.010).
findings.interpretation_limits: Associations under model; image variation could co-occur though authors report robustness excluding image RCTs.

limitations: Samples share Upworthy archive with P04 and P07; overlap size not established. Do not count as independent replications.

Same story randomized variants identify effects of packages; lexical feature coefficients are observational post-treatment classifications with possible residual wording/image confounding, despite author causal language.
Dictionary and negation heuristics do not directly measure experienced emotion; same-user exposure or demographics not available.
p4 Fig 2 caption 53,669 conflicts with Table 3 and p3 53,699; p4 complexity prose prints +0.004 with negative z and interval.
data_or_code_leads: https://osf.io/uscpf/ (paper-reported data and analysis code; not independently audited)
https://www.liwc.app/ (paper says commercial purchase; no redistribution implied)
extraction_issues: Figure 2 caption denominator conflicts with paper text/table; complexity coefficient sign typo conflicts with z and interval.

cross_paper_synthesis.shared_population: All three analyze subsets of the Upworthy Research Archive and the same historical publisher; overlap likely, exact intersection unverified, no independent replication claim. P04 8,977 image-matched bundles; P07 24,333 selected pairs; P13 12,448 filtered experiments, non-comparable denominators.
cross_paper_synthesis.causal_boundary: Randomization supports causal contrasts between complete observed packages in their experiment; language-feature attribution, moderation and nonlinearities are analyses of authored co-varying features. Cross-test mean concreteness and topics were not randomized.
cross_paper_synthesis.outcome_boundary: CTR is a choice to open a preview, not comprehension, meaningful reading, author voice, civic value or writing quality. P07 only distinguishes significantly differing pair winners.
cross_paper_synthesis.local_comparison: Local pattern test preserves varied opening routes and form purposes; calibration 21/36 original vs 18/36 revised exact sets, so proposed function refinements have no demonstrated improvement. Headline findings cannot resolve section or paragraph labels. Reuse source-aware form and audience metadata and judgment, not a universal concreteness score.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/references/structure-and-purpose.md: choose material for contribution, consider reader question; accepted-foundations F02
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Author requests a title or heading for a known form, audience and destination.
proposed_rule_changes.action: Compare whether each candidate names the contribution and gives the intended reader enough orientation; allow justified intrigue, interrogative framing or ambiguity.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Contextual title review without a single algorithmic concreteness optimum.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A reflective essay title may deliberately leave the meaning open until the ending; an API reference heading may need exact identifier.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Check declared title limits, presence/consistency of explicit terms and heading structure.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Judge fidelity, reader expectations, justified omissions and voice with author.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: skills/write-with-purpose/SKILL.md: author intent and voice, source fidelity; accepted-foundations preserve originality
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: Attention-oriented suggestion changes specificity, affect, or promises.
proposed_rule_changes.action: Review whether the title truthfully reflects the piece and the authors intended framing; do not insert negativity or omit material facts merely for CTR.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Protect source fidelity and author control.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A naturally negative title is appropriate when it faithfully describes an adverse event.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Detect mismatched named items only with supplied canonical records; check declared constraints.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Evaluate framing, emotional accuracy, fairness and relevance in full context.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: write-with-purpose: avoid generic preference for fewer words or uniformly short sentences; no default readability grade
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: A tool proposes mandatory brevity, a readability score, preferred pronoun or negative wording.
proposed_rule_changes.action: Do not use lexical signals as universal pass/fail rules.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Preserve necessary technical vocabulary, voice and functional variation.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A publisher can set an actual character ceiling; a title can be misleadingly long or short regardless of score.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Count words or characters only under declared measurement rules and enforce explicit limits.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Reader comprehension and faithful tone require assessment.

proposed_rule_changes.existing_rule: dataset-adoption plugin-reuse-notes: separate purpose, form, provenance and semantic review; calibration report indicates low function agreement
proposed_rule_changes.trigger: When a user asks the plugin to compare title options for a specific intended audience.
proposed_rule_changes.action: Offer author-chosen alternatives with stated reader question, tradeoffs and uncertainty; evaluate actual readers against intended outcomes, not just clicks.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Plausible differentiation through source-grounded, author-controlled choice.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A narrow copy-edit needs no title generation, ranking or testing workflow.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Store candidate versions, constraints and exact source links; evaluate experimental units and outcome definitions.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic: Author decides voice and goal; blinded reader task and preregistered comparison needed to demonstrate usefulness.

github_reuse.status: paper-reported leads only; not downloaded, executed, license checked or integrated
items: P04 sentence_concreteness repository and OSF registered analysis
P13 OSF analysis with separately licensed LIWC and NRC
P07 textstat reference; shared archive under its own terms
github_reuse.adoption: Any reuse needs version/license inspection, data rights and source-specific validation. No cue model should be used as an automatic style or quality evaluator.

open_questions: Can held-out human readers identify intended contribution and assess title fidelity across each target form and audience, while retaining author voice?
How much of cross-paper overlap is exact test-level overlap, and are headline/user exposures clustered across experiments?
Can an outcome-based test compare alternatives without using clickthrough as a substitute for comprehension or usefulness?
Resolve noted published denominator and numeric inconsistencies against supplements before recomputation.
